corrections.caveats: Enricher: the harness checks out (both sides scalar, DoNotOptimize symmetric), but the list is a best case: 1M nodes allocated back to back in a fresh process are likely address-ordered, so the 8x understates the usual gap. The timed loop checks for the end once per 32 accesses, valid only for element counts that are multiples of 32 (undefined behaviour otherwise). SetBytesProcessed counts 8 bytes per element for the list too, understating its memory traffic. The file includes immintrin.h unconditionally (x86 only); Chapter04 has no ReadMe.

tier_reason: C stands: first-party book figures; the committed benchmark does not compile, so the book's run used code the repo lacks.

corrections.caveats: Enricher: bench_gemm.cpp and test_gemm.cpp use ct::Matrix but never include matrix.h, so neither compiles as committed (HEAD and 0be92ac, May 2025). Both kernels bound k by B.cols() and the basic kernel bounds j by A.cols(), so results are correct only when A.cols() == B.cols(); the only test (square 250x250 all-ones) cannot catch this. Matrix a is never written, so every product is zero, and untouched fresh memory on Linux may read as the shared zero page, which can differ between runs. 289 ms is 0.29 ns per multiply-add (derived), below one floating-point add latency, so the blocked build likely got loop interchange or vectorisation (GCC -floop-interchange at -O3), which contradicts the earlier note that the gain is tile reuse alone; the ratio is likely compiler-dependent (inference, not compiled).
